nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Strong high-altitude light drives plant growth on the plateau, but nights are cold and frosty above 3,000 m.

nodes.name: Wet-season rain
nodes.desc: Rain falls mainly from May to November and feeds the grasslands, lakes and the Harenna Forest.

nodes.name: Mole-rat soil
nodes.desc: Burrowing giant root-rats loosen the ground, and the refilled tunnels hold looser, more nutrient-rich soil than the surrounding turf.

nodes.name: Soil fungi & invertebrates
nodes.desc: Break down dead grass, dung and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Afroalpine grasses
nodes.desc: Tussock grasses and herbs of the high moorland and montane grassland. They feed the root-rats, hares and grazing antelope.

nodes.name: Giant lobelia
nodes.desc: A tall rosette plant of the Afroalpine zone, found in the Bale Mountains and also in the Simien Mountains.

nodes.name: Red hot poker
nodes.desc: Tall flowering plant of the highlands. Mountain nyala eat it, and Ethiopian wolves have been seen drinking its nectar.

nodes.name: St. John's wort shrubs
nodes.desc: An evergreen mountain shrub that the mountain nyala is recorded browsing.

nodes.name: Hagenia tree
nodes.desc: A highland tree of the montane woodland whose leaves are among the foods of the mountain nyala.

nodes.name: Giant root-rat
nodes.desc: Burrowing rodent found only in the Bale highlands. It forages on grasses and herbs from burrow mouths and is the main prey of the Ethiopian wolf.

nodes.name: Grass rats
nodes.desc: Diurnal grass-eating rodents of open ground. Records near the park include Blick's and Ethiopian grass rats, which the wolf is recorded eating.

nodes.name: Ethiopian highland hare
nodes.desc: Eats moorland grasses and lives on open Afroalpine ground. The Ethiopian wolf and tawny eagle prey on it.

nodes.name: Bohor reedbuck
nodes.desc: A grazing antelope of wet grassland. Ethiopian wolves have taken reedbuck calves.

nodes.name: Common warthog
nodes.desc: A grass-eating wild pig, one of the best recorded large mammals near the park.

nodes.name: Mountain nyala
nodes.desc: Large antelope found only in the Ethiopian Highlands east of the Rift. It mostly browses herbs and shrubs, and the leopard is its main predator.

nodes.name: Ethiopian wolf
nodes.desc: Rodent specialist. In Bale it hunts mostly big-headed mole-rats. Bale holds the largest population of this endangered canid.

nodes.name: Serval
nodes.desc: A slender cat that hunts rodents, and is recorded in the park among the root-rat predators.

nodes.name: Augur buzzard
nodes.desc: A raptor commonly recorded on the plateau. It mainly eats small ground mammals such as rats and mole-rats, and reptiles.

nodes.name: African golden wolf
nodes.desc: A generalist canid that eats rodents, hares and carrion. Ethiopian wolves usually win encounters with it, though it is not a rodent specialist.

nodes.name: African leopard
nodes.desc: The main predator of the mountain nyala, living in the Harenna Forest and surrounding woodland.
